title: When Discouragement Comes to the Leader
subtitle: What Elijah under the broom tree teaches every discouraged pastor about despair in ministry, the lies exhaustion tells, and the gentle way God restores a leader who wants to quit.

sections.title: The Prophet Who Asked to Die
sections.body:
He had just won. Fire had fallen from heaven in front of the whole nation. The prophets of Baal were dead. The drought had broken. By every measure a man uses to judge a ministry, Elijah had just had the greatest day of his life.

Then a woman sent a threat, and he ran. He ran a day into the wilderness, sat under a broom tree, and asked God to let him die. It is enough, he said. Take my life. The man who had stood against four hundred and fifty prophets could not stand against a single sentence from Jezebel.

This is the thing about discouragement. It does not wait for failure. It often comes the morning after the victory, when the adrenaline drains out and the man is left alone with how tired he actually is.

sections.title: Discouragement Is a Liar With a Good Memory
sections.body:
Listen to what Elijah believed under that tree. I am the only one left. It is hopeless. I am no better than my fathers. Every word of it felt true. Not one word of it was.

He was not the only one. God had seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal, a fact Elijah could not see because despair narrows the eyes until the whole world is the size of your own pain. Discouragement does this. It takes a hard day and tells you it is a hard life. It takes one failure and calls it a verdict on your soul. It tells the pastor that no one is being reached, nothing is changing, and he might as well stop.

I have believed every one of those lies. They felt like discernment. They were exhaustion wearing the mask of truth.

sections.title: God Fed Him Before He Corrected Him
sections.body:
Notice what God did not do. He did not rebuke the prophet for his weakness. He did not give him a lecture on faith. He let him sleep. Then He fed him. Then He let him sleep again, and fed him again, because the road ahead was too great for him.

The first answer to the discouraged leader is not a sermon. It is bread and rest. So much of what we call a crisis of faith is a crisis of sleep, of food, of a body driven past what a body can bear. God is gentler with His tired servants than they are with themselves.

Only after the rest came the question. What are you doing here, Elijah. Not an accusation. An invitation back into the work, given to a man who had been fed enough to hear it.

sections.title: Not in the Wind. In the Whisper.
sections.body:
God told him to stand on the mountain. A great wind tore the rocks, but God was not in the wind. An earthquake, but God was not in the earthquake. A fire, but God was not in the fire. Then a low whisper, a sound of thin silence, and there was God.

The discouraged leader is often waiting for the dramatic rescue. The big result. The fire that fixes everything. But God most often meets the despairing not in the spectacle but in the quiet. In the whisper that says you are still mine and the work is not finished and you are not alone.

Stop straining to hear God in the storm of your circumstances. He is usually speaking under it, in a voice you have to grow still to catch.

sections.title: He Sent Him Back to Work, and Gave Him a Friend
sections.body:
God did not retire Elijah. He sent him back. There were kings to anoint and a successor to find, named Elisha, a man who would walk beside him so he would not be alone again.

That is the shape of restoration. Not a removal from the field but a return to it, lighter, with company, with the lie about being alone put to death. The discouraged pastor does not need to quit. He needs rest, bread, the whisper, and a friend, and then the slow walk back into the calling he thought was over.

You are not the only one left. You never were. Get up and eat. The road is not finished, and you do not walk it alone.
